extraction_notes.note: The proof of Lemma zeta-convexity cites Lemma \ref{zeta-convexity} itself; the intended reference is the convexity lemma (zeta-convex), added as an inferred edge.
The source uses an undeclared \begin{heuristic} environment; it was extracted as a prose claim with rigor heuristic, and its non-rigorous justification as a proof node.
These theorems (and several bounds marked \derived) are established only by computer code (\code{...} calls in the Python database), with no written proof in the source; they carry no proof node.

Many historical bounds (on mu, A(sigma), GAPMAX, GAPAA, GAPSQUARE, GAPLARGE, prime gaps, pi(x) errors) appear only as rows of literature tables; table rows were not extracted as nodes, only the theorems and remarks that cite the tables.

metadata.extraction_comment: The source is the LaTeX blueprint of a living exponent database; its \python/\code/\literature/\derived markers point to executable code and were not extracted. Many results are cited from the literature with one-line proofs that only point to the reference; these are origin external.

nodes.name: Axiom of choice
nodes.statement: We freely assume the axiom of choice in this blueprint.

nodes.name: e(theta)
nodes.statement: If $\theta$ is a real number, then we write $$ e(\theta) := e^{2\pi i\theta}$$ where $i$ is the imaginary unit.

nodes.name: Indicator function
nodes.statement: The indicator function $1_I(n)$ of a set $I$ is defined to equal $1$ when $n \in I$, and $0$ otherwise.

nodes.name: Empty supremum convention
nodes.statement: We adopt the convention that an empty supremum is $-\infty$, and an empty infimum is $+\infty$.

nodes.name: N^{-infinity} convention
nodes.statement: Related to this, we also adopt the convention that $N^{-\infty}=0$ when $N > 1$.

nodes.name: Cardinality
nodes.statement: The cardinality of a finite set $W$ will be denoted $|W|$.

nodes.name: 1-bounded sequence
nodes.statement: A sequence $a_n, n \in I$ of real or complex numbers indexed by some index set is said to be \emph{$1$-bounded} if $|a_n| \leq 1$ for all $n \in I$.
nodes.genus: sequence $a_n, n \in I$ of real or complex numbers

nodes.name: 1-separated set
nodes.statement: Similarly, a set $W$ of real numbers is said to be \emph{$1$-separated} if $|t-t'| \geq 1$ for all distinct $t,t' \in W$.

nodes.name: lambda-bounded and lambda-separated
nodes.statement: One can define more general notions of $\lambda$-bounded or $\lambda$-separated for other $\lambda>0$ in the obvious fashion.

nodes.name: Ambient index parameter
nodes.statement: In this framework, we assume there is some ambient index parameter $\ii$, which ranges over some ambient sequence of natural numbers going to infinity.

nodes.name: Fixed and variable objects
nodes.statement: All mathematical objects $X$ (numbers, sequences, sets, functions, etc.), will either be \emph{fixed} - i.e., independent of $\ii$ - or \emph{variable} - i.e., dependent on $\ii$.

nodes.name: Passing to a subsequence if necessary
nodes.statement: We will often reserve the right to refine the ambient sequence to a subsequence as needed, usually in order to apply a compactness theorem such as the Bolzano--Weierstrass theorem; we refer to this process as ``passing to a subsequence if necessary''.
nodes.definiendum: passing to a subsequence if necessary

nodes.name: Truth of variable statements
nodes.statement: When we say that a statement involving variable objects is true, we mean that it is true for all $\ii$ in the ambient sequence.

nodes.name: Variable set
nodes.statement: For instance, a variable set $E$ of real numbers is a set $E = E_{\ii}$ indexed by the ambient parameter $\ii$, and by an element of such a set, we mean a variable real number $x = x_{\ii}$ such that $x_{\ii} \in E_{\ii}$ for all $\ii$ in the ambient sequence.

nodes.name: Bounded quantity
nodes.statement: $X$ is \emph{bounded} if there exists a fixed $C$ such that $|X| \leq C$. In this case we also write $X = O(1)$.

nodes.name: Unbounded quantity
nodes.statement: $X$ is \emph{unbounded} if $|X_{\ii}| \to \infty$ as $\ii \to \infty$; equivalently, for every fixed $C$, one has $|X| \geq C$ for $\ii$ sufficiently large.

nodes.name: Infinitesimal quantity
nodes.statement: $X$ is \emph{infinitesimal} if $|X_{\ii}| \to 0$ as $\ii \to \infty$; equivalently, for every fixed $\eps>0$, one has $|X| \leq \eps$ for $\ii$ sufficiently large. In this case we also write $X = o(1)$.

nodes.name: Bounded quantities have standard parts
nodes.statement: Note that any quantity $X$ will be either bounded or unbounded, after passing to a subsequence if necessary; similarly, by the Bolzano--Weierstrass theorem, any bounded (variable) quantity $X$ will be of the form $X_0+o(1)$ for some fixed $X_0$, after passing to a subsequence if necessary. Thus, for instance, if $T, N > 1$ are (variable) quantities with $N = T^{O(1)}$ (or equivalently, $T^{-C} \leq N \leq T^C$ for some fixed $C$), then, after passing to a subsequence if necessary, we may write $N = T^{\alpha+o(1)}$ for some fixed real number $\alpha$. Note that any further passage to subsequences do not alter these concepts; quantities that are bounded, unbounded, or infinitesimal remain so under any additional restriction to subsequences.
nodes.statement_short: Every quantity is bounded or unbounded after refining; bounded ones are $X_0+o(1)$, so e.g. $N=T^{\alpha+o(1)}$ for some fixed $\alpha$.

nodes.name: Underspill principle
nodes.statement: We observe the \emph{underspill principle}: if $X,Y$ are (variable) real numbers, then the relation $$ X \leq Y + o(1)$$ is equivalent to the relation $$ X \leq Y + \eps + o(1)$$ holding for all fixed $\eps>0$.
nodes.statement_short: $X \le Y + o(1)$ iff $X \le Y + \varepsilon + o(1)$ for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$.

nodes.name: Asymptotic notation
nodes.statement: We can develop other standard asymptotic notation in the natural fashion: given two (variable) quantities $X,Y$, we write $X = O(Y)$, $X \ll Y$, or $Y \gg X$ if $|X| \leq CY$ for some fixed $C$, and $X = o(Y)$ if $|X| \leq cY$ for some infinitesimal $c$.

nodes.name: Comparable quantities
nodes.statement: We also write $X \asymp Y$ for $X \ll Y \ll X$.

nodes.name: Automatic uniformity
nodes.statement: Let $E = E_{\ii}$ be a non-empty variable set, and let $f = f_{\ii}: E \to \C$ be a variable function. \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] Suppose that $f(x)=O(1)$ for all (variable) $x \in E$. Then after passing to a subsequence if necessary, the bound is uniform, that is to say, there exists a fixed $C$ such that $|f(x)| \leq C$ for all $x \in E$. \item[(ii)] Suppose that $f(x)=o(1)$ for all (variable) $x \in E$. Then after passing to a subsequence if necessary, the bound is uniform, that is to say, there exists an infinitesimal $c$ such that $|f(x)| \leq c$ for all $x \in E$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Pointwise $O(1)$ or $o(1)$ bounds over a variable set become uniform after passing to a subsequence.
assumptions: Let $E = E_{\ii}$ be a non-empty variable set, and let $f = f_{\ii}: E \to \C$ be a variable function.
conclusions: there exists a fixed $C$ such that $|f(x)| \leq C$ for all $x \in E$.
there exists an infinitesimal $c$ such that $|f(x)| \leq c$ for all $x \in E$.
there exists a fixed $C$ such that $|f(x)| \leq C$ for all $x \in E$.
there exists an infinitesimal $c$ such that $|f(x)| \leq c$ for all $x \in E$.

nodes.label: auto

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: We begin with (i). Suppose that there is no uniform bound. Then for any fixed natural number $n$, one can find arbitrarily large $\ii_n$ in the sequence and $x_{\ii_n} \in E_{\ii_n}$ such that $|f_{\ii_n}(x_{\ii_n})| \geq n$. Clearly one can arrange matters so that the sequence $\ii_n$ is increasing. If one then restricts to this sequence and sets $x$ to be the variable element $x_{\ii_n}$ of $E$, then $f(x)$ is unbounded, a contradiction. Now we prove (ii). We can assume for each fixed $n$ that there exists $\ii_n$ in the ambient sequence such that $|f_{\ii}(x_{\ii})| \leq 1/n$ for all $\ii \geq \ii_n$ and $x_{\ii} \in E_{\ii}$, since if this were not the case one can construct an $x = x_{\ii} \in E$ such that $|f_{\ii}(x_{\ii})| \geq 1/n$ for $\ii$ sufficiently large, contradicting the hypothesis. Again, we may take the $\ii_n$ to be increasing. Restricting to this sequence, and writing $c_{\ii_n} := 1/n$, we see that $c=o(1)$ and $|f(x)| \leq c$ for all $x \in E$, as required.
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction via a diagonal sequence of indices for (i); for (ii) build the infinitesimal $c$ from an increasing index sequence.

nodes.name: Remark 1
nodes.statement: The proof gives slightly more as we only need to discard finitely many initial indices rather than pass to a subsequence which may omit infinitely many indices. Therefore, in (i), there is a fixed $C$ such that $|f_{\ii}(x)|\leq C$ for all sufficiently large $\ii$ and all $x\in E_{\ii}$. Similarly, in (ii), for every fixed $\eps>0$, one has $|f_{\ii}(x)|\leq\eps$ for all sufficiently large $\ii$ and all $x\in E_{\ii}$. Conversely, these conclusions clearly imply the corresponding hypotheses of Proposition \ref{auto}.
nodes.statement_short: In Proposition 1 one only discards finitely many initial indices, giving an eventual uniform bound; the converse also holds.

nodes.name: Remark 2
nodes.statement: It is important in Proposition \ref{auto} that the hypotheses in (i), (ii) are assumed for all \emph{variable} $x \in E$, rather than merely all \emph{fixed} $x \in E$. For instance, let $E = \R$ and consider the variable function $f_{\ii}(x) := x/\ii$. Then $f(x) = o(1)$ for any fixed $x \in E$, but the decay rate is not uniform, and we do not have $f(x) = o(1)$ for all variable $x \in E$ (e.g., $x_\ii := \ii$ is a counterexample).
nodes.statement_short: The hypotheses must hold for all variable $x$, not just fixed $x$; $f(x)=x/\ii$ is a counterexample.

nodes.name: Remark 3
nodes.statement: There are two caveats to keep in mind when using this asymptotic formalism. Firstly, the law of the excluded middle is only valid after passing to subsequences. For instance, it is possible for a nonstandard natural number to neither be even or odd, since it could be even for some $\ii$ and odd for others. However, one can pass to a subsequence in which it becomes either even or odd. Secondly, one cannot combine the ``external'' concepts of asymptotic notation with the ``internal'' framework of (variable) set theory. For instance, one cannot view the collection of all bounded (variable) real numbers as a variable set, since the notion of boundedness is not ``pointwise'' to each index $\ii$, but instead describes the ``global'' behavior of this index set. Thus, for instance, set builder notation such as $\{ x: x = O(1) \}$ should be avoided.
nodes.statement_short: Caveats: excluded middle only after passing to subsequences, and asymptotic notions cannot be used in set builder notation.

nodes.name: L^2 integral estimate
nodes.statement: Let $\xi_1,\dots,\xi_R$ be real numbers that are $1/N$-separated. Then for any interval $I$ of length $T$, and any sequence $a_1,\dots,a_R$ of complex numbers one has $$ \int_I |\sum_{r=1}^R a_r e(\xi_r t)|^2\ dt = (T + O(N)) \sum_{r=1}^R |a_r|^2.$$
nodes.statement_short: Mean value of an exponential sum with $1/N$-separated frequencies over an interval of length $T$ is $(T+O(N))\sum|a_r|^2$.
assumptions: Let $\xi_1,\dots,\xi_R$ be real numbers that are $1/N$-separated.
nodes.label: l2-int

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: We adapt the proof of \cite[Theorem 9.1]{ik}. Without loss of generality we may normalize $\sum_{r=1}^R |a_r|^2=1$. From the Plancherel identity we have \begin{equation} \int_\R |\sum_{r=1}^R a_r e(\xi_r t)|^2 |\hat \psi((t-t_0)/N)|^2\ dt = N \end{equation} whenever $t_0 \in \R$ and $\psi$ is a smooth function supported on $[-1/4, 1/4]$ of $L^2$ norm $1$. By suitable choice of $\psi$, this implies that \begin{equation} \int_J |\sum_{r=1}^R a_r e(\xi_r t)|^2\ dt \ll N \end{equation} whenever $J$ is an interval of length $N$. If one integrates \eqref{art} for all $t_0 \in I$, we see that $$ \int_I |\sum_{r=1}^R a_r e(\xi_r t)|^2\ dt = T - \int_\R |\sum_{r=1}^R a_r e(\xi_r t)|^2 \left(\frac{1}{N} \int_I |\hat \psi((t-t_0)/N)|^2\ dt_0 - 1_I(t)\right)\ dt.$$ Since $\hat \psi$ is rapidly decreasing and has $L^2$ norm $1$, one can compute $$ \frac{1}{N} \int_I |\hat \psi((t-t_0)/N)|^2\ dt_0 - 1_I(t) \ll (1 + \mathrm{dist}(t, \partial I) / N)^{-10}$$ and hence by \eqref{trap} and the triangle inequality $$ \int_\R |\sum_{r=1}^R a_r e(\xi_r t)|^2 \left(\frac{1}{N} \int_I |\hat \psi((t-t_0)/N)|^2\ dt_0 - 1_I(t)\right)\ dt \ll N$$ giving the claim.
nodes.statement_short: Plancherel with a smooth cutoff $\hat\psi$, integrated over $t_0 \in I$; the boundary error is controlled by the local bound and the triangle inequality.

nodes.name: Equation (3.1)
nodes.statement: \int_\R |\sum_{r=1}^R a_r e(\xi_r t)|^2 |\hat \psi((t-t_0)/N)|^2\ dt = N
nodes.label: art

nodes.name: Equation (3.2)
nodes.statement: \int_J |\sum_{r=1}^R a_r e(\xi_r t)|^2\ dt \ll N
nodes.label: trap

nodes.name: Phase function
nodes.statement: A \emph{phase function} is a (variable) smooth function $F \colon [1,2] \to \R$. A phase function $F$ will be called a \emph{model phase function} if there exists a fixed exponent $\sigma > 0$ with the property that \begin{equation} F^{(p+1)}(u) - \frac{d^p}{du^p} u^{-\sigma} = o(1) \end{equation} for all (variable) $u \in [1,2]$ and all fixed $p \geq 0$, where $F^{(p+1)}$ denotes the $(p+1)^{\mathrm{st}}$ derivative of $F$.
nodes.statement_short: A phase function is a smooth $F$ on $[1,2]$; it is a model phase function if its derivatives asymptotically match those of $\int u^{-\sigma}$.
nodes.label: phase-def

nodes.name: Equation (4.1)
nodes.statement: F^{(p+1)}(u) - \frac{d^p}{du^p} u^{-\sigma} = o(1)
nodes.label: fpu

nodes.name: Examples of model phase functions
nodes.statement: For instance, $u \mapsto \log u$ is a model phase function (with $\sigma=1$), and for any fixed $\sigma \neq 1$, $u \mapsto u^{1-\sigma}/(1-\sigma)$ is also a model phase function.

nodes.name: Uniform decay in model phase functions
nodes.statement: Note from Proposition \ref{auto} that the $o(1)$ decay rate in \eqref{fpu} can be made uniform, after passing to a subsequence if necessary.

nodes.name: Exponent sum growth exponent
nodes.statement: For any fixed $\alpha \geq 0$, let $\beta(\alpha) \in \R$ denote the least possible (fixed) exponent for which the following claim holds: whenever $N, T \geq 1$ are (variable) quantities with $T$ unbounded and $N = T^{\alpha+o(1)}$, $F$ is a model phase function, and $I \subset [N, 2N]$ is an interval, then $$ \sum_{n \in I} e(T F(n/N)) \ll T^{\beta(\alpha)+o(1)}.$$
nodes.statement_short: $\beta(\alpha)$ is the least exponent with $\sum_{n\in I} e(TF(n/N)) \ll T^{\beta(\alpha)+o(1)}$ for $N=T^{\alpha+o(1)}$ and model phases $F$.
nodes.label: beta-def

nodes.name: beta is well-defined
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that the set of possible candidates for $\beta(\alpha)$ is closed (thanks to underspill), non-empty, and bounded from below, so $\beta$ is well-defined as a (fixed) function from $[0,+\infty)$ to $\R$.
nodes.statement_short: The admissible exponents for $\beta(\alpha)$ form a closed, nonempty, bounded-below set, so $\beta$ is well-defined.

nodes.name: Zeta-type sums bounded by beta
nodes.statement: Specializing to the logarithmic phase $F(u) = \log u$, and performing a complex conjugation, we see in particular that \begin{equation} \sum_{n \in I} n^{-iT} \ll T^{\beta(\alpha)+o(1)} \end{equation} whenever $T$ is unbounded, $N = T^{\alpha+o(1)}$, and $I$ is an interval in $[N,2N]$.
assumptions: whenever $T$ is unbounded, $N = T^{\alpha+o(1)}$, and $I$ is an interval in $[N,2N]$.

nodes.name: Equation (4.2)
nodes.statement: \sum_{n \in I} n^{-iT} \ll T^{\beta(\alpha)+o(1)}
nodes.label: beta-alpha

nodes.name: Non-asymptotic definition of $\beta$
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha \geq 0$ and $\overline{\beta} \in \R$ be fixed. Then the following are equivalent: \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] $\beta(\alpha) \leq \overline{\beta}$. \item[(ii)] For every (fixed) $\eps>0$ and $\sigma > 0$ there exists (fixed) $\delta>0$, $P \geq 1$, $C \geq 1$ with the following property: if $T \geq C$, $T^{\alpha-\delta} \leq N \leq T^{\alpha+\delta}$ are (fixed) real numbers, $I \subset [N,2N]$ is a (fixed) interval, and $F$ is a (fixed) phase function such that \begin{equation} \left|F^{(p+1)}(u) - \frac{d^p}{du^p} u^{-\sigma}\right| \leq \delta \end{equation} for all (fixed) $0 \leq p \leq P$ and $u \in [1,2]$, then $$ |\sum_{n \in I} e(T F(n/N))| \leq C T^{\overline{\beta}+\eps}.$$ \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: $\beta(\alpha)\le\bar\beta$ iff an explicit epsilon-delta exponential sum bound holds for all phases close to model ones.
equivalent_conditions: For every (fixed) $\eps>0$ and $\sigma > 0$ there exists (fixed) $\delta>0$, $P \geq 1$, $C \geq 1$ with the following property
nodes.label: beta-asymp

nodes.name: Equation (4.3)
nodes.statement: \left|F^{(p+1)}(u) - \frac{d^p}{du^p} u^{-\sigma}\right| \leq \delta
nodes.label: fpu-bound

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that (ii) implies (i) by expanding out all the definitions (and using Proposition \ref{auto} to resolve any uniformity issues). Conversely, suppose that (ii) fails. Carefully negating all the quantifiers, we conclude that there exists a fixed $\eps, \sigma > 0$ such that for any (fixed) natural number $\ii$, one can find real numbers $T = T_{\ii} \geq \ii$, $T^{\alpha-1/\ii} \leq N = N_{\ii} \leq T^{\alpha+1/\ii}$, an interval $I = I_{\ii} \subset [N_\ii, 2N_\ii]$, and a phase function $F = F_{\ii}$ such that $$ |F_\ii^{(p+1)}(u) - \frac{d^p}{du^p} u^{-\sigma}| \leq 1/\ii$$ for all (fixed) $0 \leq p \leq \ii$ and $u \in [1,2]$, but that $$ |\sum_{n \in I} e(T F(n/N))| \geq \ii T^{\overline{\beta}+\eps}.$$ But then $F = F_\ii$ is a model phase function which gives a counterexample to the claim $\beta(\alpha) \leq \overline{\beta}$.
nodes.statement_short: Unpack the definitions for (ii)$\Rightarrow$(i); for the converse negate (ii) and assemble a model phase function counterexample.

nodes.name: Trivial bounds on beta
nodes.statement: For any fixed $\alpha > 1$, we have $$ \beta(\alpha) = \alpha-1.$$ For fixed $0 \leq \alpha \leq 1$, we have $$ \frac{\alpha}{2} \leq \beta(\alpha) \leq \alpha.$$ In particular \begin{equation} \beta(0)=0. \end{equation}
nodes.label: beta-triv

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $T > 1$ be unbounded, $N = T^{\alpha+o(1)}$, $I \subset [N,2N]$ an interval, and $F$ a model phase function. For $\alpha > 1$, the Euler--Maclaurin formula (see e.g. \cite[(2.1.2)]{titchmarsh_theory_1986}) gives \begin{equation} \left|\sum_{N \leq n \leq 2N} n^{iT}\right| = \left|\frac{2^{1+iT} - 1}{1+iT} N^{1+iT} + O(1)\right| \asymp \frac{N}{T} \end{equation} which gives the lower bound $\beta(\alpha) \geq \alpha-1$; applying the Euler--Maclaurin formula for model phase functions $F$ then gives the matching upper bound. The triangle inequality bound $$ \sum_{n \in I} e(T F(n/N)) \ll N$$ gives the upper bound $\beta(\alpha) \leq \alpha$. Next, if $0 \leq \alpha \leq 1$, then from Lemma \ref{l2-int} (and the $\gg 1/N$-separated nature of the $F(n/N)$ for model phase functions $F$, after passing to a subsequence if necessary) that $$ \int_T^{2T} \left|\sum_{n \in [N,2N]} e(t F(n/N)) \right|^2\, dt \asymp T N$$ for $N = cT^\alpha$ for $c$ a fixed small enough constant, which by the pigeonhole principle implies that $$\left| \sum_{n \in [N,2N]}e(t F(n/N)) \right| \gg N^{1/2} = T^{\alpha/2}$$ for at least one $t \asymp T$, giving the claim.
nodes.statement_short: Euler--Maclaurin for $\alpha>1$, the triangle inequality for the upper bound, and the $L^2$ estimate plus pigeonholing for the lower bound $\alpha/2$.

nodes.name: Equation (4.5)
nodes.statement: \left|\sum_{N \leq n \leq 2N} n^{iT}\right| = \left|\frac{2^{1+iT} - 1}{1+iT} N^{1+iT} + O(1)\right| \asymp \frac{N}{T}
nodes.label: nit

nodes.name: Conjectured value of beta
nodes.statement: As we shall see, the exponent pair conjecture is equivalent to the lower bound here being sharp, thus it is conjectured that \[ \beta(\alpha) = \begin{cases} \alpha/2,& 0 \leq \alpha \leq 1\\ \alpha - 1,&\alpha > 1 \end{cases}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Conjecture: $\beta(\alpha)=\alpha/2$ on $[0,1]$ and $\alpha-1$ for $\alpha>1$ (equivalent to the exponent pair conjecture).

nodes.name: Upper semicontinuity
nodes.statement: $\beta$ is an upper semicontinuous function.
nodes.label: beta-semicts

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Routine from the definition.

nodes.name: Van der Corput A process for beta
nodes.statement: If $0 \leq \alpha \leq 2/3$ and $h \geq 0$ then $$ 2\beta(\alpha) \leq \max\left( 2\alpha - h, 2h, \alpha - h + \sup_{2\alpha-1 \leq h' \leq h} \left((h'+1-\alpha)\beta\left(\frac{\alpha}{h'+1-\alpha}\right)+h'\right)\right).$$
nodes.statement_short: Weyl differencing (A-process) bounds $2\beta(\alpha)$ by a max over shift sizes $h'$ of $\beta$ at a transformed argument.
nodes.label: vdca-beta

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: By definition, there exists an unbounded $T$, $N = T^{\alpha+o(1)}$, $F$ a model phase function, and $I \subset [N,2N]$ such that $$ \sum_{n \in I} e(T F(n/N)) = T^{\beta(\alpha)+o(1)}.$$ Applying \cite[(2.54)]{ivic} with $H := T^h$, as well as the ensuing computations to dispose of the $j \ll T/N^2$ terms, one then has $$ T^{2\beta(\alpha)+o(1)} \ll N^2 H^{-1} + H^2 + N H^{-1} \sum_{T/N^2 \ll j \ll H} |\sum_{n \in I \cap I-j} e(T (F((n+j)/N) - F(n/N)))|$$ and hence by the pigeonhole principle $$ T^{2\beta(\alpha)+o(1)} \ll N^2 H^{-1} + H^2 + T^{o(1)} N H^{-1} \sum_{j = T^{h'+o(1)}} |\sum_{n \in I \cap I-h} e(T (F((n+j)/N) - F(n/N)))|$$ for some $2\alpha-1 \leq h' \leq h$ (one can delete this term if $h < 2\alpha-1$). One can verify that $-\frac{1}{\sigma} \frac{N}{j} (F(u+j/N)-F(u/N))$ is a model phase function. Thus, by Definition \ref{beta-def}, one has $$ \sum_{n \in I \cap I-h} e(T (F((n+j)/N) - F(n/N))) \ll (T^{1+h'+o(1)}/N)^{\beta(\alpha/(h'+1-\alpha))+o(1)},$$ and the claim follows after evaluating all terms as powers of $T$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Weyl differencing (Ivic (2.54)) with $H=T^h$, pigeonhole the shift $j$, and bound the differenced sums by the definition of $\beta$.

nodes.name: Van der Corput inequality
nodes.statement: For any natural number $k \geq 2$ and any $\alpha>0$, one has $$ \beta(\alpha) \leq \max\left( \alpha + \frac{1-k\alpha}{2^k-2}, (1 - 2^{2-k})\alpha - \frac{1-\alpha}{2^k-2}\right).$$ Thus for instance when $k=2$ we have $$ \beta(\alpha) \leq \max\left( \frac{1}{2}, \frac{2\alpha-1}{2} \right),$$ so in particular \begin{equation} \beta(1)= \frac{1}{2}, \end{equation} by Lemma \ref{beta-triv}, when $k=3$ one has $$ \beta(\alpha) \leq \max\left( \frac{1+3\alpha}{6}, \frac{6\alpha-1}{3} \right),$$ and when $k=4$ one has $$ \beta(\alpha) \leq \max\left( \frac{10\alpha+1}{14}, \frac{29\alpha-2}{28} \right).$$
nodes.statement_short: Classical $k$-th derivative test: $\beta(\alpha)$ bounded by a max of two linear functions of $\alpha$, with cases $k=2,3,4$ and $\beta(1)=1/2$.
assumptions: For any natural number $k \geq 2$ and any $\alpha>0$
nodes.label: beta-vdc

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Follows from \cite[Theorem 8.20]{ik}. It is also possible to prove this by induction on $k$ using Lemma \ref{vdca-beta}.
nodes.statement_short: Cited from Iwaniec--Kowalski; alternatively induction on $k$ via the A-process lemma.

nodes.name: Optimizing the van der Corput inequality
nodes.statement: For any $\alpha > 0$ one has $$\beta(\alpha) \leq \inf_{k \in \N: k \geq 2} \alpha + \frac{1-k\alpha}{2^k-2}.$$ Thus for instance $$ \beta(\alpha) \leq \min\left( \frac{1}{2}, \frac{1+3\alpha}{6}, \frac{10\alpha+1}{14}\right).$$
nodes.label: vdc-opt

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $\beta_k(\alpha) = \alpha + (1 - k\alpha)/(2^k - 2)$ and \[ \alpha_k = \frac{2^k}{(k - 1)2^k + 2}. \] Via a routine computation, $\beta_k(\alpha) \le \beta_{k+1}(\alpha)$ for $\alpha \ge \alpha_k$ and any $k \ge 2$. Thus, to verify that $\beta(\alpha) \le \beta_k(\alpha)$ for $0 \le \alpha \le 1/2$, it suffices to just show that the same result holds for $0 \le \alpha \le \alpha_{k}$. However, for $0 \le \alpha \le \alpha_k$ and $k \ge 2$, we have \[ 0 \le \alpha \le \alpha_k \le \frac{2^{k + 1}}{(k - 3)2^k + 8} \] which rearranges to give \[ \alpha + \frac{1-k\alpha}{2^k-2}\geq (1 - 2^{2-k})\alpha - \frac{1-\alpha}{2^k-2},\qquad (0 \le \alpha \le \alpha_k, k \ge 2) \] which completes the proof in view of Proposition \ref{beta-vdc}. See Figure \ref{fig:vdc}.
nodes.statement_short: Compare consecutive bounds $\beta_k$ via the threshold $\alpha_k$ and check the first term dominates the max in Proposition 4 below $\alpha_k$.

nodes.name: Lemma 6
nodes.statement: In Definition \ref{beta-def}, one can take the interval $I$ to be $[N,2N]$.
nodes.statement_short: The interval $I$ in the definition of $\beta$ may be taken to be $[N,2N]$.
conclusions: In Definition \ref{beta-def}, one can take the interval $I$ to be $[N,2N]$.
nodes.label: interval-set

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\alpha, \overline{\beta}$ are fixed quantities such that the bounds in Definition \ref{beta-def} hold just for $I = [N,2N]$, thus whenever $T>1$ is unbounded, $N = T^{\alpha+o(1)}$, and $F$ is a model phase function one has \begin{equation} \sum_{N \leq n \leq 2N} e(T F(n/N)) \ll T^{\overline{\beta}+o(1)}. \end{equation} Our task is then to show that $$ \sum_{n \in I} e(T fF(n/N)) \ll T^{\overline{\beta}+o(1)}$$ under the same hypotheses. Similarly with $\alpha=1$ we can use the proof of Lemma \ref{beta-vdc} to obtain $\overline{\beta} \geq 1/2$, and we are again done. Thus we may assume that $\alpha < 1$. For $n \in [N,2N]$, the constraint $n \in I$ is equivalent to restricting $F(n/N)$ to an interval $J$ of length $O(1)$, which we can also smooth out by $O(1/N)$ without affecting the sum. Applying a Fourier expansion and the triangle inequality, we can thus bound the left-hand side by $$ \ll T^{o(1)} + \int_{-N^{1+o(1)}}^{N^{1+o(1)}} \left|\sum_{n \in [N,2N]} e(T F(n/N) - t F(n/N)) \right| \frac{dt}{1+|t|}.$$ Since $\alpha > 1$, we have $|t-T| \leq T/2$ for all $t$ in the integral if $T$ is large enough. From hypothesis \eqref{three} (with $T$ replaced by $T-t$)we have $$ \left|\sum_{n \in [N,2N]} e(T F(n/N) - t F(n/N)) \right| \ll T^{\overline{\beta}+o(1)}$$ for all such $t$, and the claim follows. See also Sargos \cite[p 310]{sargos_points_1995}.
nodes.statement_short: Fourier-expand the indicator of the subinterval and apply the full-interval hypothesis at shifted frequencies $T-t$.

nodes.name: Equation (4.7)
nodes.statement: \sum_{N \leq n \leq 2N} e(T F(n/N)) \ll T^{\overline{\beta}+o(1)}.
nodes.label: three

nodes.name: Reflection
nodes.statement: For any $0 < \alpha < 1$, we have $\beta(\alpha) - \frac{\alpha}{2} = \beta(1-\alpha) - \frac{1-\alpha}{2}$, or equivalently $\beta(1-\alpha) = \frac{1}{2} - \alpha + \beta(\alpha)$.
nodes.statement_short: Van der Corput B-process: $\beta(\alpha)-\alpha/2$ is symmetric under $\alpha\mapsto 1-\alpha$.
nodes.origin_citation: van der Corput B-process; Huxley 1996, p. 370
nodes.label: beta-reflect

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: This is the van der Corput $B$-process. See e.g., \cite[p 370]{huxley_area_1996}.

nodes.name: Corollary also follows from van der Corput classification
nodes.statement: We remark that this corollary also follows from Proposition \ref{vdc-class}.

nodes.name: 1989 Watt bound
nodes.statement: For any $3/7 \le \alpha \le 1/2$, one has \[ \beta(\alpha) \le \frac{89}{560} + \frac{1}{2}\alpha. \]
nodes.label: beta-Watt

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: See \cite[Theorem~5]{watt_exponential_1989}.

nodes.name: 1991 Huxley--Kolesnik bound
nodes.statement: For any $2/5 \le \alpha \le 1/2$ one has \[ \beta(\alpha) \le \max\left(\frac{1 + 8\alpha}{22}, \frac{11 + 112\alpha}{158}, \frac{1 + 17\alpha}{22}\right). \]
nodes.label: beta-HK2

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: See \cite[Theorem~3]{huxley_exponential_1991}. Note that the paper contains an error, however this result was reinstated with the corrections given in \cite{huxley_exponential_1993_1}.

nodes.name: 1993 Huxley bound
nodes.statement: For any $0 \le \alpha \le 49/114$, one has \[ \beta(\alpha) \le \max\left(\frac{13}{60} + \frac{7}{20}\alpha, \frac{11}{120} + \frac{13}{20}\alpha\right). \] Furthermore, for any $49/114 \le \alpha \le 1/2$, one has \[ \beta(\alpha) \le \frac{89}{570} + \frac{1}{2}\alpha. \]
nodes.label: beta-Huxley-4

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: See \cite[Theorem~1]{huxley_exponential_1993}.

nodes.name: Second 1993 Huxley bound
nodes.statement: If $0 \leq \alpha \leq 1$, then $\beta(\alpha)$ is bounded by \begin{align*} \frac{1}{146} (13+94\alpha) & \hbox{ for } \alpha \leq \frac{87}{275} \\ \frac{1}{244} (11+191\alpha) & \hbox{ for } \frac{87}{275} \leq \alpha \leq \frac{423}{1295} \\ \frac{1}{1282} (89+908\alpha) & \hbox{ for } \frac{423}{1295} \leq \alpha \leq \frac{227}{601} \\ \frac{1}{280} (29+173\alpha) & \hbox{ for } \frac{227}{601} \leq \alpha \leq \frac{12}{31} \\ \frac{1}{128} (4+103\alpha) & \hbox{ for } \frac{12}{31} \leq \alpha \leq 1. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Piecewise-linear bound on $\beta(\alpha)$ over five ranges of $\alpha\in[0,1]$.
nodes.label: beta-Huxley-4a

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: See \cite[Theorem~3]{huxley_exponential_1993}.

nodes.name: 1995 Sargos bound
nodes.statement: \cite[Th\'eor\`eme 2.4, Lemme 2.6]{sargos_points_1995} For any $0 \leq \alpha \leq 1$, one has $$ \beta(\alpha) \leq \max\left(\alpha + \frac{3(1-4\alpha)}{40}, \frac{7}{8} \alpha, \frac{1}{3}\alpha - \frac{1-4\alpha}{6}, 0\right)$$ and $$ \beta(\alpha) \leq \max\left(\alpha + \frac{1-4\alpha}{14}, \frac{5}{6} \alpha, \frac{1}{3}\alpha - \frac{1-4\alpha}{6}, 0\right).$$
nodes.label: sargos_1995

nodes.name: 1996 Huxley table
nodes.statement: One can bound $\beta(\alpha)$ by $\beta_0(\alpha)$ for $X \leq \alpha \leq Y$ for $\beta_0, X, Y$ given by Tables \ref{huxley-table-1}, \ref{huxley-table-2}.
nodes.statement_short: Piecewise-linear bounds $\beta\le\beta_0$ on ranges $[X,Y]$ from Huxley's tables.
nodes.label: huxley-table

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: See \cite[Table 17.1, Table 19.2]{huxley_area_1996} (and also \cite[\S 3.0.2, 3.0.3]{trudgian-yang} for some verification of the technical conditions on the phase).

nodes.name: 2001 Huxley--Kolesnik bound
nodes.statement: For any $2/5 \le \alpha \le 1/2$ one has $$ \beta(\alpha) \leq \max\left(\frac{7}{80} + \frac{79}{120}\alpha, \frac{3}{32} + \frac{103}{160}\alpha, \frac{9}{40} + \frac{13}{40}\alpha\right).$$
nodes.label: beta-HK

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: See \cite[Theorem~1]{huxley_exponential_2001}.

nodes.name: 2002 Robert--Sargos bound
nodes.statement: For any $\alpha > 0$ one has $$ \beta(\alpha) \leq \max\left( \alpha + \frac{1-4\alpha}{13}, -\frac{7(1-4\alpha)}{13}\right).$$
nodes.label: beta-RS

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: See \cite[Theorem~1]{robert_fourth_2002}.

nodes.name: Sargos 2003 bound
nodes.statement: For any $\alpha > 0$ one has $$ \beta(\alpha) \leq \max\left( \alpha + \frac{1-8\alpha}{204}, -\frac{95(1-8\alpha)}{204}\right)$$ and $$ \beta(\alpha) \leq \max\left( \alpha + \frac{7(1-9\alpha)}{2640}, -\frac{1001(1-9\alpha)}{2640}\right).$$
nodes.label: sargos-bound

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: See \cite[Theorems~3, 4]{sargos_analog_2003}.

nodes.name: Huxley bound
nodes.statement: For any $1/3 \le \alpha \le 1/2$, one has \[ \beta(\alpha) \le \max\left(\frac{37 + 59\alpha}{170}, \frac{63 + 449\alpha}{690}\right). \]
nodes.label: beta-Huxley-5

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: See \cite[Proposition~1, Theorem~1]{huxley_exponential_2005}.

nodes.name: 2016 Robert bound
nodes.statement: For any $0 < \alpha \le 3/7$ one has \[ \beta(\alpha) \le \max\left(\alpha + \frac{1 - 4\alpha}{12}, \frac{11}{12}\alpha\right). \]
nodes.label: beta-R

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: See \cite[Theorem~1]{robert_fourth_2016}.

nodes.name: Second 2016 Robert bound
nodes.statement: If $k \geq 4$ and $\alpha \geq -(1-k\alpha) \frac{k-1}{2k-3}$ then $$ \beta(\alpha) \leq \alpha + \max( \frac{1-k\alpha}{2(k-1)(k-2)}, -\frac{1}{2(k-1)(k-2)}).$$
nodes.label: beta-R2

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: See \cite[Theorem 10]{robert_2016}.

nodes.name: 2017 Heath-Brown bound
nodes.statement: For any $\alpha > 0$ and any natural number $k \geq 3$ one has $$ \beta(\alpha) \leq \alpha + \max\left( \frac{1-k\alpha}{k(k-1)}, -\frac{\alpha}{k(k-1)}, -\frac{2\alpha}{k(k-1)} - \frac{2(1-k\alpha)}{k^2(k-1)}\right).$$
assumptions: For any $\alpha > 0$ and any natural number $k \geq 3$
nodes.label: beta-HB

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: See \cite[Theorem~1]{heathbrown_new_2017}.

nodes.name: 2017 Bourgain bound
nodes.statement: One has \[ \beta(\alpha) \le \begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{2}{9} + \frac{1}{3}\alpha,&\displaystyle\frac{1}{3} < \alpha \le \frac{5}{12},\\ \\ \displaystyle\frac{1}{12} + \frac{2}{3}\alpha,&\displaystyle\frac{5}{12} < \alpha \le \frac{3}{7},\\ \\ \displaystyle\frac{13}{84} + \frac{1}{2}\alpha,&\displaystyle\frac{3}{7} < \alpha \le \frac{1}{2}. \end{cases} \]
nodes.statement_short: Bourgain's decoupling bound: piecewise linear bound on $\beta(\alpha)$ for $1/3<\alpha\le1/2$.
nodes.label: beta-Bourgain

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: See \cite[Equation~(3.18)]{bourgain_decoupling_2017}.

nodes.name: 2020 Heath-Brown bound
nodes.statement: If $\alpha$ is fixed with $1 \leq 4\alpha-1 \leq 2$ (i.e., $1/2 \leq \alpha \leq 3/4$), then $$ \beta(\alpha) \leq \max\left( \alpha\left(1 - \frac{4\alpha-1}{4(4\alpha-1)+8}\right), \frac{8}{9} \alpha\right).$$
nodes.label: beta-hb-2020

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: See \cite[Theorem 11.2]{demeter_small_2020}.

nodes.name: Combined bound
nodes.statement: For $X \leq \alpha \leq Y$, one has $\beta(\alpha) \leq \beta_0(\alpha)$, where $\beta_0, X, Y$ are given by Table \ref{huxley_table_ranges}.
nodes.statement_short: Combined piecewise-linear bound on $\beta(\alpha)$ from the table of best known bounds.
nodes.label: combined-bound

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: See \cite[Table 3]{trudgian-yang}.

nodes.name: Exponent pair
nodes.statement: An exponent pair is a (fixed) element $(k,\ell)$ of the triangle \begin{equation} \{ (k,\ell) \in \R^2: 0 \leq k \leq 1/2 \leq \ell \leq 1, k+\ell \leq 1 \} \end{equation} with the following property: for all model phase functions $F$, all $T \geq N \geq 1$, and all intervals $I \subset [N,2N]$, one has \begin{equation} \sum_{n \in I} e(T F(n/N)) \ll (T/N)^{k+o(1)} N^{\ell+o(1)} \end{equation} whenever $T \geq N \geq 1$, $I$ is an interval in $[N,2N]$, and $F \in {\mathcal U}$.
nodes.statement_short: $(k,\ell)$ in the triangle is an exponent pair if $\sum_{n\in I} e(TF(n/N)) \ll (T/N)^{k+o(1)}N^{\ell+o(1)}$ for all model phases.
nodes.label: exp-pair-def

nodes.name: Exponent pair triangle
nodes.statement: \{ (k,\ell) \in \R^2: 0 \leq k \leq 1/2 \leq \ell \leq 1, k+\ell \leq 1 \}
nodes.label: exp-pair-triangle

nodes.name: Equation (5.2)
nodes.statement: \sum_{n \in I} e(T F(n/N)) \ll (T/N)^{k+o(1)} N^{\ell+o(1)}
nodes.label: ntf

nodes.name: Non-asymptotic definition of exponent pair
nodes.statement: Let $(k,\ell)$ be a fixed element of \eqref{exp-pair-triangle}. Then the following are equivalent: \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] $(k,\ell)$ is an exponent pair. \item[(ii)] For every (fixed) $\eps>0$ there exist (fixed) $C, P > 0$ such that, whenever $T \geq N \geq 1$, $I \subset [N,2N]$, and $F$ is a phase function obeying \eqref{fpu-bound} for all (fixed) $0 \leq p \leq P$ and $u \in [1,2]$, then $$ |\sum_{n \in I} e(T F(n/N))| \leq C (T/N)^{k+\eps} N^{\ell+\eps}.$$ \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Being an exponent pair is equivalent to an explicit epsilon-dependent exponential sum bound for nearly-model phases.
assumptions: Let $(k,\ell)$ be a fixed element of \eqref{exp-pair-triangle}.
equivalent_conditions: For every (fixed) $\eps>0$ there exist (fixed) $C, P > 0$ such that

nodes.name: Proof of non-asymptotic exponent pair lemma
nodes.statement: The proof of this lemma is similar to that of Lemma \ref{beta-asymp} and is omitted.
nodes.statement_short: Same as the proof of the non-asymptotic definition of $\beta$ (omitted).

nodes.name: Duality between exponent pairs and beta
nodes.statement: Let $(k,\ell)$ be in the triangle \eqref{exp-pair-triangle}. Then the following are equivalent: \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] $(k,\ell)$ is an exponent pair. \item[(ii)] $\beta(\alpha) \leq k + (\ell-k)\alpha$ for all $0 \leq \alpha \leq 1$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: $(k,\ell)$ is an exponent pair iff $\beta(\alpha) \le k+(\ell-k)\alpha$ on $[0,1]$.
nodes.label: beta-duality

nodes.name: Exponent pairs dual to convex hull of beta
nodes.statement: Thus exponent pairs are dual to the convex hull of the graph of $\beta$. But $\beta$ is not known to be convex, so one could have bounds on $\beta$ that do not directly correspond to exponent pairs.

nodes.name: Half-range check in duality
nodes.statement: We remark that in the case $\ell - k \geq 1/2$, one only needs to check the case $0 \leq \alpha \leq 1/2$ in (ii) above, since the remaining regime $1/2 \leq \alpha \leq 1$ then follows from Lemma \ref{beta-reflect} and some algebra. Conversely, if $\ell - k \leq 1/2$, one only needs to check the region $1/2 \leq \alpha \leq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: If $\ell-k\ge1/2$ only $\alpha\le1/2$ needs checking in duality (reflection gives the rest); if $\ell-k\le1/2$ only $\alpha\ge1/2$.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: If (i) holds, then for any $0 < \alpha < 1$, any unbounded $T \geq 1$, any $N = T^{\alpha+o(1)}$, interval $I \subset [N,2N]$, and model phase function $F$, we have from (i) that $$ \sum_{n \in I} e(T F(n/N)) \ll (T/N)^{k+o(1)} N^{\ell+o(1)} = T^{k + (\ell-k)\alpha + o(1)}.$$ From Definition \ref{beta-def} we conclude that $\beta(\alpha) \leq k + (\ell-k) \alpha$. Also since $(k,\ell)$ lies in \eqref{exp-pair-triangle}, we see from \eqref{beta-0}, \eqref{beta-1} that we also have $\beta(\alpha) \leq k + (\ell-k) \alpha$ for $\alpha=0,1$. Now suppose that (ii) holds. Let $F, T, N, I$ be as in Definition \ref{exp-pair-def}. By underspill it suffices to show that $$ \sum_{n \in I} e(T F(n/N)) \ll (T/N)^{k+\eps+o(1)} N^{\ell+\eps+o(1)}$$ for any fixed $\eps>0$. We may assume that $T \leq N^{1/\eps+1}$, since the claim follows from the trivial bound $\sum_{n \in I} e(T F(n/N)) \ll N$ otherwise. We may also assume that $N$ is unbounded, since the claim is clear for $N$ bounded; this forces $T$ to be unbounded as well. By passing to a subsequence we may assume that $N = T^{\alpha+o(1)}$ for some fixed $0 \leq \alpha \leq 1$. By Definition \ref{beta-def} we then have $$ \sum_{n \in I} e(T F(n/N)) \ll T^{\beta(\alpha)+o(1)}$$ and hence by (ii) $$ \sum_{n \in I} e(T F(n/N)) \ll (T/N)^{k+o(1)} N^{\ell+o(1)}$$ giving the claim.
nodes.statement_short: (i)$\Rightarrow$(ii) by the definition of $\beta$; (ii)$\Rightarrow$(i) by underspill, reductions to unbounded $N$, and $N=T^{\alpha+o(1)}$.

nodes.name: Exponent pairs closed and convex
nodes.statement: The set of exponent pairs is closed and convex.
conclusions: The set of exponent pairs is closed and convex.
nodes.label: exp-pair-closed

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Immediate from Lemma \ref{beta-duality}.

nodes.name: Trivial exponent pairs
nodes.statement: $(0,1)$ and $(1/2,1/2)$ are exponent pairs.
nodes.label: exp-pair-trivial

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Immediate from Lemma \ref{beta-duality} and Lemma \ref{beta-triv}.
nodes.statement_short: Duality plus the trivial bounds on $\beta$.

nodes.name: Exponent pairs conjecture
nodes.statement: $(0,1/2)$ is an exponent pair. (Equivalently, by Corollary \ref{exp-pair-closed} and Proposition \ref{exp-pair-trivial}, every point in the triangle \eqref{exp-pair-triangle} is an exponent pair.)
nodes.statement_short: $(0,1/2)$ is an exponent pair; equivalently every point of the triangle is.
nodes.label: exp-pair-conj

nodes.name: Lemma 10
nodes.statement: The exponent pair conjecture is equivalent to $\beta(\alpha)=\alpha/2$ holding true for all $0 \leq \alpha \leq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: The exponent pair conjecture is equivalent to $\beta(\alpha)=\alpha/2$ on $[0,1]$.
conclusions: The exponent pair conjecture is equivalent to $\beta(\alpha)=\alpha/2$ holding true for all $0 \leq \alpha \leq 1$.
nodes.label: exp-pair-conj-beta

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Clear from Lemma \ref{beta-duality} and Lemma \ref{beta-triv}.
nodes.statement_short: Duality plus the trivial bounds on $\beta$.

nodes.name: Van der Corput A-process
nodes.statement: If $(k,\ell)$ is an exponent pair, then so is $$A(k,\ell) := \left(\frac{k}{2k+2}, \frac{\ell}{2k+2} + \frac{1}{2}\right).$$
nodes.statement_short: The A-process $A(k,\ell)=(k/(2k+2), \ell/(2k+2)+1/2)$ maps exponent pairs to exponent pairs.
nodes.label: vdc-a

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: See \cite[Lemma 2.8]{ivic}. It can also be deduced from Lemma \ref{vdca-beta} and Lemma \ref{beta-duality}.
nodes.statement_short: Cited (Ivic Lemma 2.8); alternatively from the A-process for $\beta$ and duality.

nodes.name: Van der Corput B-process
nodes.statement: If $(k,\ell)$ is an exponent pair, then so is $$B(k,\ell) := \left(\ell-\frac{1}{2}, k+\frac{1}{2}\right).$$
nodes.statement_short: The B-process $B(k,\ell)=(\ell-1/2, k+1/2)$ maps exponent pairs to exponent pairs.
nodes.label: vdc-b

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: See \cite[Lemma 2.9]{ivic}. Alternatively, this can be derived from Lemma \ref{beta-reflect} and Lemma \ref{beta-duality}.
nodes.statement_short: Cited (Ivic Lemma 2.9); alternatively from reflection for $\beta$ and duality.

nodes.name: Classical van der Corput exponent pairs
nodes.statement: For any natural number $k \geq 2$, $$ A^{k-2} B(0,1) = \left( \frac{1}{2^k-2}, 1 - \frac{k-1}{2^k-2} \right)$$ is an exponent pair. In particular, $$ \left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right), \left(\frac{1}{6}, \frac{2}{3}\right), \left(\frac{1}{14}, \frac{11}{14}\right)$$ are exponent pairs.
nodes.statement_short: $A^{k-2}B(0,1) = (1/(2^k-2), 1-(k-1)/(2^k-2))$ is an exponent pair for every $k\ge2$.
nodes.label: vdc-class

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Follows by induction from Proposition \ref{vdc-a} and Proposition \ref{exp-pair-trivial}; alternatively, follows from (and is equivalent to) Corollary \ref{vdc-opt} and Lemma \ref{beta-duality}.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $k$ using the A-process from the trivial pair; alternatively from the optimized van der Corput bound and duality.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: We have $(2/7,4/7) = BA(1/6,2/3)$, $(4/18,11/18) = BABA(1/6,2/3)$, and $(13/31, 16/31)=BAB^2A^2(1/6,2/3)$, so these cases follow from Propositions \ref{vdc-class}, \ref{vdc-a}, \ref{vdc-b}. Finally, $(4/11,6/11)$ is a convex combination of $(1/2,1/2)$ and $(2/7,4/7)$, and $(5/24, 15/24)$ is a convex combination of $(1/6,2/3)$ and $(4/18, 11/18)$, so these cases follow from Corollary \ref{exp-pair-closed}.
nodes.statement_short: Write three pairs as $A$/$B$ words applied to $(1/6,2/3)$ and the other two as convex combinations.

nodes.name: Growth rate of zeta
nodes.statement: For any fixed $\sigma \in \R$, let $\mu(\sigma)$ denote the least possible (fixed) exponent for which one has the bound $$ |\zeta(\sigma+it)| \ll |t|^{\mu(\sigma)+o(1)}$$ for all unbounded $t$.
nodes.section: 6 Growth exponents for the Riemann zeta function
nodes.label: zeta-grow-def

nodes.name: mu is well-defined
nodes.statement: One can check that for each $\sigma$, the set of possible candidates for $\mu(\sigma)$ is closed (by underspill), non-empty, and bounded from below, so that $\mu(\sigma)$ is well-defined as a real number.
nodes.section: 6 Growth exponents for the Riemann zeta function

nodes.name: Non-asymptotic characterization of mu
nodes.statement: An equivalent definition without asymptotic notation, is that $\mu(\sigma)$ is the least real number such that for every $\eps>0$ there exists $C>0$ such that $$ |\zeta(\sigma+it)| \leq C |t|^{\mu(\sigma)+\eps}$$ for all $t$ with $|t| \geq C$; equivalently, one has $$ \mu(\sigma) = \limsup_{|t| \to \infty} \frac{\log |\zeta(\sigma+it)|}{\log|t|}.$$
nodes.section: 6 Growth exponents for the Riemann zeta function
nodes.statement_short: $\mu(\sigma)$ equals the least exponent in an explicit $\varepsilon$-$C$ bound, i.e. $\limsup \log|\zeta(\sigma+it)|/\log|t|$.

nodes.name: Trivial bound
nodes.statement: One has $\mu(\sigma)=0$ for all $\sigma \geq 1$.
nodes.section: 6 Growth exponents for the Riemann zeta function
nodes.label: zeta-grow-triv

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Immediate from the absolute convergence of the Dirichlet series for both $\zeta(s)$ and $1/\zeta(s)$; see e.g., \cite[Theorem 1.9]{ivic}.
nodes.section: 6 Growth exponents for the Riemann zeta function
nodes.statement_short: Absolute convergence of the Dirichlet series of $\zeta$ and $1/\zeta$.

nodes.name: Convexity
nodes.statement: $\mu$ is convex.
nodes.section: 6 Growth exponents for the Riemann zeta function
nodes.label: zeta-convex

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Immediate from the Phragm\'en--Lindel\"of principle; see e.g., \cite[\S A.8]{ivic}.
nodes.section: 6 Growth exponents for the Riemann zeta function

nodes.name: Functional equation
nodes.statement: One has $\mu(1-\sigma) = \mu(\sigma) + \sigma - 1/2$ for all $0 \leq \sigma \leq 1/2$.
nodes.section: 6 Growth exponents for the Riemann zeta function
nodes.label: zeta-functional

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Immediate from the functional equation for $\zeta$ and asymptotics of the Gamma function; see e.g., \cite[(1.23), (1.25)]{ivic}.
nodes.section: 6 Growth exponents for the Riemann zeta function
nodes.statement_short: Functional equation of $\zeta$ and Gamma function asymptotics.

nodes.name: Left of critical strip
nodes.statement: One has $\mu(\sigma)=1/2-\sigma$ for $\sigma \leq 0$.
nodes.section: 6 Growth exponents for the Riemann zeta function
nodes.label: zeta-left

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Immediate from Lemmas \ref{zeta-grow-triv}, \ref{zeta-functional}.
nodes.section: 6 Growth exponents for the Riemann zeta function
nodes.statement_short: Combine the trivial bound with the functional equation.

nodes.name: Convexity bounds
nodes.statement: One has $\max(0, 1/2-\sigma) \leq \mu(\sigma) \leq (1-\sigma)/2$ for $0 \leq \sigma \leq 1$.
nodes.section: 6 Growth exponents for the Riemann zeta function
nodes.label: zeta-convexity

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Immediate from Lemma \ref{zeta-grow-triv}, Lemma \ref{zeta-left}, and Lemma \ref{zeta-convexity}.
nodes.section: 6 Growth exponents for the Riemann zeta function
nodes.statement_short: Combine the trivial bound, the bound left of the strip, and convexity of $\mu$.

nodes.name: Connection with dual exponent pairs
nodes.statement: For any $1/2 \leq \sigma \leq 1$, one has $$ \mu(\sigma) \leq \sup_{0 \leq \alpha \leq 1/2} \beta(\alpha) - \alpha \sigma.$$
nodes.section: 6.1 Connection with exponent pairs and dual exponent pairs
nodes.label: mu-beta

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $t$ be unbounded. From the Riemann--Siegel formula (see \cite[Theorem 4.1]{ivic}) one has $$ \zeta(\sigma+it) \ll \left|\sum_{n \leq \sqrt{t/2\pi}} \frac{1}{n^{\sigma+it}}\right| + |t|^{1/2-\sigma} \left|\sum_{n \leq \sqrt{t/2\pi}} \frac{1}{n^{1-\sigma-it}}\right| + O(1).$$ From dyadic decomposition and Definition \ref{beta-def} (and Lemma \ref{auto}) one has for any fixed $\eps>0$ that $$\sum_{t^\eps \leq n \leq \sqrt{t/2\pi}} \frac{1}{n^{\sigma+it}} \ll |t|^{\sup_{\eps \leq \alpha \leq 1/2} \beta(\alpha) - \alpha \sigma + o(1)},$$ while from the triangle inequality one has the crude bound $$\sum_{n < t^\eps} \frac{1}{n^{\sigma+it}} \ll |t|^\eps.$$ Combining the bounds and using underspill, we conclude that $$\sum_{n \leq \sqrt{t/2\pi}} \frac{1}{n^{\sigma+it}} \ll |t|^{\sup_{0 \leq \alpha \leq 1/2} \beta(\alpha) - \alpha \sigma + o(1)}.$$ A similar argument gives $$\sum_{n \leq \sqrt{t/2\pi}} \frac{1}{n^{1-\sigma-it}} \ll |t|^{\sup_{0 \leq \alpha \leq 1/2} \beta(\alpha) - \alpha (1-\sigma) + o(1)}$$ Since $\sigma \geq 1/2$ and $\alpha \leq 1/2$, one has $(1/2-\sigma) - \alpha(1-\sigma) \leq -\alpha \sigma$, and hence $$ \zeta(\sigma+it) \ll |t|^{\sup_{0 \leq \alpha \leq 1/2} \beta(\alpha) - \alpha \sigma + o(1)}$$ giving the claim.
nodes.section: 6.1 Connection with exponent pairs and dual exponent pairs
nodes.statement_short: Riemann--Siegel formula, then dyadic decomposition and the definition of $\beta$ for each of the two sums.

nodes.name: mu-beta inequality is morally an equality
nodes.statement: We remark that this inequality is morally an equality (indeed, it would be if one would restrict the model phases in Definition \ref{beta-def} to purely the logarithmic phase $u \mapsto \log u$).
nodes.section: 6.1 Connection with exponent pairs and dual exponent pairs

nodes.name: Exponent pairs and mu
nodes.statement: If $(k,\ell)$ is an exponent pair, then $$ \mu(\ell-k) \leq k.$$

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Immediate from Lemma \ref{mu-beta} and Lemma \ref{beta-duality}. See also \cite[(7.57)]{ivic}.

nodes.name: Lindelof hypothesis
nodes.statement: One has $\mu(1/2)=0$.
nodes.section: 6.1 Connection with exponent pairs and dual exponent pairs
nodes.label: LH

nodes.name: Lemma 17
nodes.statement: The exponent pair conjecture implies the Lindel\"of hypothesis.
nodes.section: 6.1 Connection with exponent pairs and dual exponent pairs
nodes.statement_short: The exponent pair conjecture implies the Lindelof hypothesis.
nodes.label: exp-pair_implies_lindelof

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Immediate from Corollary \ref{exp-pair-mu}.
nodes.section: 6.1 Connection with exponent pairs and dual exponent pairs
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the corollary relating exponent pairs and $\mu$.

nodes.name: Conjectured value of mu
nodes.statement: We have the lower bound \begin{equation} \mu(\sigma) \geq \max\left(0, \frac{1}{2}-\sigma\right) \end{equation} for all $\sigma \in \R$, and equality holds everywhere in \eqref{muh} if and only if the Lindel\"of hypothesis holds.
nodes.section: 6.1 Connection with exponent pairs and dual exponent pairs
nodes.statement_short: $\mu(\sigma)\ge\max(0,1/2-\sigma)$, with equality everywhere iff the Lindelof hypothesis holds.
conclusions: equality holds everywhere in \eqref{muh} if and only if the Lindel\"of hypothesis holds.
nodes.label: mu-conj

nodes.name: Equation (6.1)
nodes.statement: \mu(\sigma) \geq \max\left(0, \frac{1}{2}-\sigma\right)
nodes.section: 6.1 Connection with exponent pairs and dual exponent pairs
nodes.label: muh

nodes.name: No further lower bounds on mu
nodes.statement: We remark that this proposition explains why there are no further lower bounds on $\mu$ in the literature beyond \eqref{muh}; all the remaining known results revolve around upper bounds.
nodes.section: 6.1 Connection with exponent pairs and dual exponent pairs

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Clearly equality in \eqref{muh} implies the Lindel\"of hypothesis, while from the trivial bounds in Propositions \ref{zeta-grow-triv}, \ref{zeta-left} and convexity (Lemma \ref{zeta-convexity}) one we see that the Lindel\"of hypothesis implies the upper bound $$ \mu(\sigma) \leq \max\left(0, \frac{1}{2}-\sigma\right)$$ for all $\sigma$. So it suffices to establish the lower bound unconditionally. By the functional equation (Proposition \ref{zeta-functional}) it suffices to do this for $\sigma \geq 1/2$; in fact by convexity it suffices to establish the claim when $1/2 < \sigma < 1$. In this regime, the $L^2$ mean value theorem (see \cite[Theorem 1.11]{ivic}) gives $$ \int_0^T |\zeta(\sigma+it)|^2\ dt \asymp T$$ for large $T$, giving the claim.
nodes.section: 6.1 Connection with exponent pairs and dual exponent pairs
nodes.statement_short: LH plus convexity gives the upper bound; the lower bound reduces to $1/2<\sigma<1$ where the $L^2$ mean value theorem applies.

nodes.name: Historical bounds
nodes.statement: The upper bounds on $\mu(\sigma)$ given by Table \ref{mu-table} are known.

nodes.name: Trudgian--Yang mu bounds
nodes.statement_short: Piecewise-linear and $(1-\sigma)^{3/2}$-type upper bounds on $\mu(\sigma)$ for $1/2\le\sigma\le1$.

nodes.name: Heath-Brown mu bounds
nodes.statement: For any integer $k \ge 3$, one has \[ \mu\left(1 - \frac{3 k^2 - 3 k + 2}{k(k - 1)^2(k + 2)}\right)\le \frac{2}{(k - 1)^2(k + 2)}. \]

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Follows from substituting \Cref{heath-brown_exp_pair_2017} into \eqref{exp-pair-mu}.

nodes.name: Sharpest known bounds on mu
nodes.statement: The new exponent pairs in \Cref{new-exp-pair} may be used to obtain sharper bounds on $\mu(\sigma)$ in certain ranges. The current sharpest bounds on $\mu(\sigma)$ are recorded in \Cref{best-mu-table} and graphed in \Cref{fig:best_mu_bound}.

nodes.name: Riemann hypothesis implies Lindelof hypothesis
nodes.statement: It is well known that the Riemann hypothesis implies the Lindel\"of hypothesis.

nodes.name: Growth exponent and zeroes
nodes.statement: Let $1/2 \leq \sigma_0 < 1$ be fixed. Then the assertion $\mu(\sigma_0)=0$ is equivalent to the assertion that for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$ and unbounded $T>0$, the number of zeroes $\sigma+it$ of the zeta function with $\sigma \geq \sigma_0+\varepsilon$ and $T \leq t \leq T+1$ is $o(\log T)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mu(\sigma_0)=0$ iff zeta has $o(\log T)$ zeros with $\sigma\ge\sigma_0+\varepsilon$ in each window $[T,T+1]$.
conclusions: the assertion $\mu(\sigma_0)=0$ is equivalent to the assertion that for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$ and unbounded $T>0$, the number of zeroes $\sigma+it$ of the zeta function with $\sigma \geq \sigma_0+\varepsilon$ and $T \leq t \leq T+1$ is $o(\log T)$.
equivalent_conditions: the number of zeroes $\sigma+it$ of the zeta function with $\sigma \geq \sigma_0+\varepsilon$ and $T \leq t \leq T+1$ is $o(\log T)$

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: This is a routine adaptation of Theorem 2 of \url{https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2015/03/01}.
nodes.statement_short: Routine adaptation of an argument from Tao's blog.

nodes.name: Large value pattern
nodes.statement: A \emph{large value pattern} is a tuple $(N, T, V, (a_n)_{n \in [N,2N]}, J, W)$, where $N > 1$ and $T, V > 0$ are real numbers, $a_n$ is a $1$-bounded sequence on $[N,2N]$, $J$ is an interval of length $T$, and $W$ is a $1$-separated subset of $J$ such that \begin{equation} \left|\sum_{n \in [N,2N]} a_n n^{-it} \right| \geq V \end{equation} for all $t \in W$. A \emph{Zeta large value pattern} is a large value pattern in which $J = [T,2T]$ and $a_n = 1_I(n)$ for some interval $I \subset [N,2N]$.
nodes.statement_short: A large value pattern is data $(N,T,V,a_n,J,W)$ with $W$ a 1-separated set where the Dirichlet polynomial exceeds $V$; zeta patterns have $a_n=1_I(n)$.
nodes.label: large-pattern-def

nodes.name: Equation (7.1)
nodes.statement: \left|\sum_{n \in [N,2N]} a_n n^{-it} \right| \geq V
nodes.label: V-large

nodes.name: Translation invariance of large value patterns
nodes.statement: The choice of interval $J$ is not too important for a large value pattern, since one can translate $J$ and $W$ by any shift $t_0$ if we also modulate the coefficients $a_n$ by $n^{it_0}$ to compensate. However, this modulation freedom is not available for zeta large value patterns, as it destroys the form $a_n = 1_I(n)$ of the coefficients.

nodes.name: R = |W|
nodes.statement: The cardinality $|W|$ of $W$ is traditionally called $R$ in the literature.

nodes.name: Relaxations of boundedness and separation
nodes.statement: It is common in the literature to relax the $1$-boundedness hypothesis on $a_n$ slightly, for instance to $a_n \ll T^{o(1)}$, but this does not significantly affect the analysis here. Similarly, the $1$-separation hypothesis is sometimes strengthened slightly to a $\lambda$-separation hypothesis for some $\lambda = T^{o(1)}$, but again this does not make much difference.

nodes.name: Second moment G
nodes.statement: For some estimates, the uniform bound on $a_n$ can be relaxed to an $\ell^2$ hypothesis $\sum_{n \in [N,2N]} |a_n|^2 \ll N$ (and this second moment is traditionally called $G$ in the literature), but we will not study such relaxations systematically here, as they are less relevant for the theory of zero density estimates.

nodes.name: Large value exponent
nodes.statement: Let $1/2 \leq \sigma \leq 1$ and $\tau \geq 0$ be fixed. We define $\LV(\sigma,\tau)$ to be the least fixed quantity for which the following claim is true: whenever $(N,T,V,(a_n)_{n \in [N,2N]},J,W)$ is a large value pattern with $N>1$ unbounded, $T = N^{\tau+o(1)}$, and $V = N^{\sigma+o(1)}$, then $$ |W| \ll N^{\LV(\sigma,\tau)+o(1)}.$$
nodes.statement_short: $\LV(\sigma,\tau)$ is the least exponent with $|W| \ll N^{\LV(\sigma,\tau)+o(1)}$ for large value patterns with $T=N^{\tau}$, $V=N^{\sigma}$.
nodes.label: lv-def

nodes.name: LV is well-defined
nodes.statement: One can check that the set of possible candidates for $\LV(\sigma,\tau)$ is closed (by underspill), non-empty, and bounded from below, so $\LV(\sigma,\tau)$ is well-defined as a real number.

nodes.name: Asymptotic form of large value exponent
nodes.statement: Let $1/2 \leq \sigma \leq 1$, $\tau \geq 0$, and $\rho \geq 0$ be fixed. Then the following are equivalent: \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] $\LV(\sigma,\tau) \leq \rho$. \item[(ii)] For every (fixed) $\eps>0$ there exists $C, \delta>0$ such that if $(N,T,V,(a_n)_{n \in [N,2N]},J,W)$ is a large value pattern with $N \geq C$ and $N^{\tau-\delta} \leq T \leq N^{\tau+\delta}$, $N^{\sigma-\delta} \leq V \leq N^{\sigma+\delta}$, then one has $$ |W| \leq C N^{\rho+\eps}.$$ \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: $\LV(\sigma,\tau)\le\rho$ iff an explicit $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ bound $|W|\le CN^{\rho+\varepsilon}$ holds.
equivalent_conditions: For every (fixed)  $\eps>0$ there exists $C, \delta>0$ such that
nodes.label: lv-asymp

nodes.name: Proof of asymptotic form of LV
nodes.statement: The proof of Lemma \ref{lv-asymp} is similar to that of Lemma \ref{beta-asymp}, and is left to the reader.
nodes.statement_short: As for the non-asymptotic definition of $\beta$ (left to the reader).

nodes.name: Basic properties of LV
nodes.statement: \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] (Monotonicity in $\sigma$) For any $\tau \geq 0$, $\sigma \mapsto \LV(\sigma,\tau)$ is upper semicontinuous and monotone non-increasing. \item[(ii)] (Huxley subdivision) For any $1/2 \leq \sigma \leq 1$ and $\tau' \geq \tau$ one has $$ \LV(\sigma,\tau) \leq \LV(\sigma,\tau') \leq \LV(\sigma,\tau) + \tau'-\tau.$$ In particular, $\tau \mapsto \LV(\sigma,\tau)$ is Lipschitz continuous. \item[(iii)] ($\tau=0$ endpoint) One has $\LV(\sigma,0)=0$ for all $1/2 \leq \sigma \leq 1$, and hence by (ii) $0 \leq \LV(\sigma,\tau) \leq \tau$ for all $1/2 \leq \sigma \leq 1$ and $\tau \geq 0$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: $\LV$ is monotone in $\sigma$, Lipschitz in $\tau$ (Huxley subdivision), and $\LV(\sigma,0)=0$, so $0\le\LV\le\tau$.
nodes.label: lv-basic

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: All claims are clear except perhaps for the upper bound $$ \LV(\sigma,\tau') \leq \LV(\sigma,\tau) + \tau'-\tau,$$ but this follows because any interval of length $N^{\tau'+o(1)}$ may be subdivided into $N^{\tau'-\tau+o(1)}$ intervals of length $N^{\tau+o(1)}$, so on applying Definition \ref{lv-def} to each subinterval and summing (using Lemma \ref{auto} to ensure uniformity), one obtains the claim.
nodes.statement_short: Subdivide an interval of length $N^{\tau'}$ into $N^{\tau'-\tau}$ subintervals and sum the bounds.

nodes.name: Lower bound on LV
nodes.statement: For any $1/2 < \sigma \leq 1$ and $\tau \geq 0$, one has $\LV(\sigma, \tau) \geq \min(2 - 2 \sigma,\tau)$, while for $\sigma=1/2$ one has $\LV(\sigma,\tau) = \tau$.
nodes.label: lv-lower

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: In view of Lemma \ref{lv-basic}(ii), it suffices to show that $\LV(\sigma, 2-2\sigma) \geq 2-2\sigma$. By definition, it suffices to find a large value pattern $(N,T,V,(a_n)_{n \in [N,2N]},J,W)$ is a large value pattern with $N$ unbounded, $V=N^{\sigma+o(1)}$, $T = N^{2-2\sigma+o(1)}$, and $|W| \gg N^{2-2\sigma-o(1)}$. In the endpoint case $\sigma = 1$ one can achieve this by setting $a_n=1$ for all $n$ and taking $W=\{0\}$, so now we assume that $1/2 < \sigma<1$. We use the probabilistic method. We divide $[N,2N]$ into $\asymp N^{2-2\sigma}$ intervals $I$ of length $\asymp N^{2\sigma-1}$. On each interval $I$, we choose $a_n$ to equal some randomly chosen sign $\epsilon_I \in \{-1,+1\}$, with the $\epsilon_I$ chosen independently in $I$. If $t = o(N^{2-2\sigma})$, then $\sum_{n \in I} a_n n^{-it}$ is equal to $\epsilon_I$ times a deterministic quantity $c_{t,I}$ of magnitude $\asymp N^{2\sigma-1}$ (the point being that the phase $t \log n$ is close to constant in this range). By the Chernoff bound, we thus see that for any such $t$, $\sum_{n \in [N,2N]} a_n n^{it}$ will have size $\gg N^{(2\sigma-1) + (2-2\sigma)/2} = N^\sigma$ with probability $\gg 1$. By linearity of expectation, we thus see that with positive probability, a $\gg 1$ fraction of integers $t$ with $t = o(N^{2-2\sigma})$ will have this property, giving the claim. Finally, let $\sigma=1/2$. In this case we just take each $a_n$ to be a random sign, then by the Chernoff bound one has for each $t$ that $|\sum_{n \in [N,2N]} a_n n^{it}| \asymp N^{1/2}$ with positive probability, which by linearity of expectation as before gives the lower bound $\LV(\sigma,\tau) \geq \tau$, while the upper bound is trivial from Lemma \ref{lv-basic}(iii).
nodes.statement_short: Probabilistic construction: random signs on blocks of length $N^{2\sigma-1}$ and the Chernoff bound give many large values.

nodes.name: Montgomery conjecture
nodes.statement: One has \begin{equation} \LV(\sigma, \tau) \leq 2 - 2 \sigma \end{equation} for all fixed $1/2 < \sigma \leq 1$ and $\tau \geq 0$. Equivalently (by Lemma \ref{lv-basic}(ii), (iii) and Lemma \ref{lv-lower}), one has $\LV(\sigma, \tau) = \min(2 - 2 \sigma,\tau)$ for all $1/2 < \sigma \leq 1$ and $\tau \geq 0$.
nodes.label: montgomery-conj

nodes.name: Equation (7.2)
nodes.statement: \LV(\sigma, \tau) \leq 2 - 2 \sigma
nodes.label: mont-conj

nodes.name: Discussion of the Montgomery conjecture
nodes.statement: We refer to \cite{bourgain_montgomery_1991} for further discussion of this conjecture, including some counterexamples to strong versions of the conjecture in which certain epsilon losses are omitted. In view of this conjecture, we do not expect any further lower bounds on $\LV(\sigma,\tau)$ to be proven, and the literature is instead focused on upper bounds.

nodes.name: Subdivision and the Montgomery conjecture
nodes.statement: If $\sigma$ is fixed, and the Montgomery conjecture holds for all fixed $\tau < \tau_0$, then \begin{equation} \LV(\sigma, \tau) \leq \max( 2 - 2 \sigma, \tau - \tau_0 + 2 - 2\sigma) \end{equation} for all fixed $\tau \geq 0$.
assumptions: If $\sigma$ is fixed, and the Montgomery conjecture holds for all fixed $\tau < \tau_0$
nodes.label: montgomery-subdivide

nodes.name: Equation (7.3)
nodes.statement: \LV(\sigma, \tau) \leq \max( 2 - 2 \sigma, \tau - \tau_0 + 2 - 2\sigma)
nodes.label: lvt-opt

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Clear from Lemma \ref{lv-basic}(ii).

nodes.name: Raising to a power
nodes.statement: For any $1/2 \leq \sigma \leq 1$, $\tau \geq 0$, and natural number $k$, one has $$ \LV(\sigma, k\tau) \leq k \LV(\sigma, \tau).$$
nodes.label: power-lemma

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $(N,T,V,(a_n)_{n \in [N,2N]},J,W)$ be a large value pattern with $T = N^{k\tau+o(1)}$ and $V = N^{\sigma+o(1)}$, Raising \eqref{V-large} the $k^{\mathrm{th}}$ power, we conclude that $$ \left|\sum_{n \in [N^k,2^kN^k]} b_n n^{-it} \right| \geq V^k$$ for all $t \in W$, where $b_n$ is the Dirichlet convolution of $k$ copies of $a_n$, and thus is bounded by $N^{o(1)}$ thanks to divisor bounds. Subdividing $[N^k, 2^k N^k]$ into $k$ intervals of the form $[N',2N']$ for $N' \asymp N^k$ and applying Definition \ref{lv-def} (with $N, T, V$ replaced by $N', T, V^k$) we conclude that $$ |W| \ll N^{k \LV(\sigma,\tau) + o(1)}$$ and the claim then follows.
nodes.statement_short: Raise the Dirichlet polynomial to the $k$-th power (divisor bound on coefficients) and apply the definition at length $N^k$.

nodes.name: Large value theorems
nodes.statement: Similarly to upper bounds on $\beta(\alpha)$, upper bounds on $\LV(\sigma,\tau)$ in the literature (also known as \emph{large value theorems}) tend to be piecewise linear functions of $\sigma$ and $\tau$.

nodes.name: Shape of large value bounds
nodes.statement: Such bounds often tend to be convex initially (i.e., the maximum of several linear functions), but when one combines multiple large value theorems together, the bound is usually neither convex nor concave, though it often remains piecewise linear, and continuous in $\tau$ (though jump discontinuities in $\sigma$ are possible).

nodes.name: L^2 mean value theorem
nodes.statement: For any fixed $1/2 \leq \sigma \leq 1$ and $\tau\geq 0$ one has $$ \LV(\sigma,\tau) \leq \max( 2-2\sigma, 1 + \tau - 2 \sigma).$$ In particular, the Montgomery conjecture \eqref{mont-conj} holds for $\tau \leq 1$.
nodes.label: l2-mvt

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $(N,T,V,(a_n)_{n \in [N,2N]},J,W)$ be a large value pattern with $T = N^{\tau + o(1)}$, $V = N^{\sigma + o(1)}$. Applying \cite[Theorem~9.4]{ik} (with $N$, $T$ replaced with $2N$, $2T$ respectively and taking $a_n = 0$ for $n < N$) one has \[ |W|V^2 \le \sum_{t \in W} \left|\sum_{N \le n \le 2N} a_n n^{-it}\right|^2 \ll N^{1 + o(1)}(T + N) \] from which the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the mean value theorem for Dirichlet polynomials (Iwaniec--Kowalski Thm 9.4) at the points of $W$.

nodes.name: Montgomery large values theorem
nodes.statement: If $1/2 \leq \sigma \leq 1$ and $\tau \geq 0$ is such that \begin{equation} \sup_{1 \leq \tau' \leq \tau} \beta(1/\tau') \tau' < 2\sigma - 1 \end{equation} (this condition is vacuous for $\tau < 1$) then the Montgomery conjecture \eqref{mont-conj} holds for this choice of parameters.
conclusions: then the Montgomery conjecture \eqref{mont-conj} holds for this choice of parameters.
nodes.label: montgomery-lv

nodes.name: Equation (7.4)
nodes.statement: \sup_{1 \leq \tau' \leq \tau} \beta(1/\tau') \tau' < 2\sigma - 1
nodes.label: tab

nodes.name: Pointer to Halasz--Montgomery
nodes.statement: For a stronger version of this inequality, see Lemma \ref{hl-improv}.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Set $\rho := \LV(\sigma,\tau)$; we may assume without loss of generality that $\rho \geq 0$. Then by Definition \ref{lv-def}, we can find a large value pattern $(N,T,V,(a_n)_{n \in [N,2N]},J,W)$ with $N > 1$ unbounded, $T = N^{\tau + o(1)}$, $V = N^{\sigma + o(1)}$, and $|W| = N^{\rho+o(1)}$. From \eqref{V-large} we have $$ \sum_{t \in W} \left|\sum_{n \in [N,2N]} a_n n^{it} \right| \geq |W|V$$ hence for some $1$-bounded coefficients $c_t$ $$ \left|\sum_{t \in W} c_t \sum_{n \in [N,2N]} a_n n^{it} \right| \geq |W|V$$ We apply the Hal\'asz argument. Interchanging the summations and applying Cauchy--Schwarz, we conclude that $$ |W|V \leq N^{1/2} \left|\sum_{t, t' \in W} c_t \overline{c_{t'}} \sum_{n \in [N,2N]} n^{i(t-t')} \right|^{1/2}$$ hence on squaring and using the triangle inequality $$ N^{2\rho} \ll N^{1-2\sigma+o(1)} \sum_{t,t' \in W} \left|\sum_{n \in [N,2N]} n^{i(t-t')} \right|.$$ In the case $|t - t'| \leq N^{1-\eps}$ for any fixed $\eps>0$, one can use Lemma \ref{beta-triv} to obtain the bound $$ \sum_{n \in [N,2N]} n^{i(t-t')} \ll N^{o(1)} \frac{N}{1 + |t - t'|}.$$ The total contribution of this case can then be bounded by $N^{1+o(1)} R = N^{1+\rho+o(1)}$, thanks to the $1$-separation. In the remaining cases $|t - t'| \geq N^{1-o(1)}$, we use Definition \ref{beta-def} to see that $$ \sum_{n \in [N,2N]} n^{i(t-t')} \ll N^{\sup_{1 \leq \tau' \leq \tau} \beta(1/\tau') \tau' + o(1)}$$ and thus $$ N^{2\rho} \ll N^{2-2\sigma+\rho+o(1)} + N^{2\rho + 1-2\sigma+\sup_{1 \leq \tau' \leq \tau} \beta(1/\tau') \tau' + o(1)}.$$ By hypothesis, the second term on the right-hand side is asymptotically smaller than the left-hand side, and so we obtain $\rho \leq 2-2\sigma$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: Halasz duality argument: Cauchy--Schwarz, then bound the off-diagonal sums by the trivial bound for close $t,t'$ and by $\beta$ for far ones.

nodes.name: Converting an exponent pair to a large values theorem
nodes.statement: If $(k,\ell)$ is an exponent pair, and $1/2 \leq \sigma \leq 1$, and $\tau \geq 0$ are fixed, then $$\LV(\sigma,\tau) \leq \max\left( 2-2\sigma, 2 - 2\sigma + \tau - \frac{2\sigma+k-\ell-1}{k} \right).$$ In particular, the Montgomery conjecture holds for $\tau \leq \frac{2\sigma+k-\ell-1}{k}$.
assumptions: If $(k,\ell)$ is an exponent pair, and $1/2 \leq \sigma \leq 1$, and $\tau \geq 0$ are fixed
nodes.label: exp-lv

nodes.name: Pointer to mu-to-large-values
nodes.statement: One can also obtain a similar implication starting from a bound on $\mu$: see Lemma \ref{mu-lv}.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{montgomery-subdivide} it suffices to prove the latter claim. From Lemma \ref{beta-duality} one has $\beta(1/\tau') \tau' \leq k \tau' + (\ell-k)$ and so the condition \eqref{tab} holds whenever $$ \tau < \frac{2\sigma+k-\ell-1}{k}.$$ The claim follows.
nodes.statement_short: By subdivision reduce to the Montgomery range, then verify the hypothesis of Montgomery's theorem via duality.

nodes.name: Huxley large values theorem
nodes.statement: \cite[Equation~(2.9)]{Huxley} Let $1/2 \leq \sigma \leq 1$ and $\tau \geq 0$ be fixed. Then one has $$ \LV(\sigma,\tau) \leq \max( 2-2\sigma, 4 + \tau - 6 \sigma).$$ In particular, one has the Montgomery conjecture for $\tau \leq 4 \sigma - 2$.
nodes.label: huxley-lv

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Apply Corollary \ref{exp-lv} with the pair $(k,\ell) = (1/2,1/2)$ from Lemma \ref{vdc-class}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the exponent-pair large values corollary with $(1/2,1/2)$.

nodes.name: Heath-Brown large values theorem, preliminary form
nodes.statement: Let $1/2 \leq \sigma \leq 1$ and $\tau \geq 0$ be fixed. If $\LV(\sigma, \tau) \le \rho$ then \[ \LV(\sigma, \tau) \le \max\left(2 - 2\sigma, \frac{11}{12}\rho + \frac{3}{2} + \frac{\tau}{6} - 2\sigma\right) \]
nodes.label: heath_brown-lv-prelim

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Follows from \cite[Lemma~1]{heathbrown_zero_1979}.

nodes.name: Heath-Brown large values theorem, optimized
nodes.statement: Let $1/2 \leq \sigma \leq 1$ and $\tau \geq 0$ be fixed. One has $$ \LV(\sigma,\tau) \leq \max( 2-2\sigma, 10 + \tau - 13 \sigma).$$ In particular, the Montgomery conjecture holds for $\tau \leq 11 \sigma - 8$.
nodes.label: hb-opt

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{montgomery-subdivide} it suffices to show that $\LV(\sigma,\tau) \leq 2-2\sigma$ for $\tau \leq 11\sigma-8$. From the previous theorem, and setting $\rho = \LV(\sigma,\tau)$, we have either $$ \LV(\sigma,\tau) \leq 2-2\sigma$$ or $$ \LV(\sigma,\tau) \leq \frac{11}{12}\LV(\sigma,\tau) + \frac{3}{2} + \frac{\tau}{6} - 2\sigma.$$ The latter bound can be rearranged as $$ \LV(\sigma,\tau) \leq 2\tau + 18 - 24\sigma$$ and thus $$ \LV(\sigma,\tau) \leq \min( 2-2\sigma, 2\tau + 18 - 24\sigma),$$ and the claim follows. (See also the arguments in the first paragraph of \cite[p. 226]{heathbrown_zero_1979}.)
nodes.statement_short: Apply the preliminary form with $\rho=\LV(\sigma,\tau)$ and solve the resulting self-improving inequality.

nodes.name: Second Heath-Brown large values theorem
nodes.statement: If $3/4 < \sigma \leq 1$ and $\tau \geq 0$ are fixed, then $$ \LV(\sigma,\tau) \leq \max( 2-2\sigma, k\tau + k(2-4\sigma), 2\tau/3 + k(12-16\sigma)/3 )$$ for any positive integer $k$.
nodes.label: hb-lvt-2

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $(N,T,V,(a_n)_{n \in [N,2N]},J,W)$ be a large value pattern with $N \geq 1$ be unbounded, $T = N^{\tau + o(1)}$, $V = N^{\sigma + o(1)}$, and $|W| = N^{\rho+o(1)}$. By \cite[Lemma~6]{heathbrown_large_1979} we have $$ (|W| V)^2 \ll T^{o(1)}( |W|N + |W|^2 N^{1/2} + |W|^{2-1/2k} T^{1/2} + |W|^{2-3/8k} N^{1/2} T^{1/4k}) N$$ and thus $$ 2(\rho + \sigma) \leq \max( \rho+1, 2\rho+1/2, (2-1/2k)\rho + \tau/2, (2-3/8k)\rho + 1/2 + \tau/4k).$$ Since $\sigma > 3/4$, we can delete the second term $2\rho+1/2$ on the right-hand side. Solving for $\rho$, we conclude that $$ \rho \leq \max( 2-2\sigma, k\tau + k(2-4\sigma), 2\tau/3 + k(12-16\sigma)/3 ),$$ and taking suprema in $\rho$, we obtain the claim.
nodes.statement_short: Insert Heath-Brown's Lemma 6 inequality, drop a term using $\sigma>3/4$, and solve for $\rho$.

nodes.name: Jutila large values theorem
nodes.statement: For any integer $k \geq 1$, one has $$ \LV(\sigma,\tau) \leq \max(2-2\sigma, \tau + (4-2/k) - (6-2/k)\sigma, \tau + (6-8\sigma)k).$$ Thus for instance with $k=2$ we have $$ \LV(\sigma,\tau) \leq \max(2-2\sigma, \tau + 3 - 5\sigma, \tau + 12-16\sigma)$$ and with $k=3$ we have $$ \LV(\sigma,\tau) \leq \max(2-2\sigma, \tau + \frac{10-16\sigma}{3}, \tau + 18-24\sigma).$$ In particular, the Montgomery conjecture holds for $$ \tau \leq \min( (4-2/k)\sigma - (2-2/k), (8k-2)\sigma - 6k + 2).$$
nodes.label: jutila-lvt

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: See \cite[(1.4)]{jutila_zero_density_1977} (setting $V = N^{\sigma+o(1)}$, $T = N^{\tau+o(1)}$, and $G \leq N$). We remark that this form is an optimized form of the inequality after (3.2) in Jutila's paper, which in our notation would read that $$ 2\LV(\sigma,\tau) + 2\sigma \leq \max \left(2 + \rho, \frac{3}{2} + \left(2 - \frac{1}{k}\right)\rho + \rho + \frac{1}{2k}\max\left(k(\tau-1), \frac{\rho+\tau}{2}\right), 2\rho + 1\right)$$ whenever $\LV(\sigma,\tau) \leq \rho$. The optimization follows from Lemma \ref{montgomery-subdivide} and routine calculations.
nodes.statement_short: Cited from Jutila, with the optimized form obtained via subdivision.

nodes.name: Large value zeta exponent
nodes.statement: Let $1/2 \leq \sigma \leq 1$ and $\tau \geq 0$ be fixed. We define $\LV_\zeta(\sigma,\tau) \in [-\infty, +\infty)$ to be the least (fixed) exponent for which the following claim is true: if $(N,T,V,(a_n)_{n \in [N,2N]},J,W)$ is a zeta large value pattern with $N$ is unbounded, $T = N^{\tau+o(1)}$, and $V = N^{\sigma+o(1)}$, then $|W| \ll N^{\rho+o(1)}$.
nodes.section: 8 Large value theorems for zeta partial sums
nodes.statement_short: $\LV_\zeta(\sigma,\tau)$ is the large value exponent restricted to zeta large value patterns.
nodes.label: lvz-def

nodes.name: Relevant ranges of tau
nodes.statement: We will primarily be interested in the regime $\tau \geq 2$ (as this is the region connected to the Riemann-Siegel formula for $\zeta(\sigma+it)$), but for sake of completeness we develop the theory for the entire range $\tau \geq 0$. (The range $0 \leq \tau \leq 1$ can be worked out exactly by existing tools, while the region $1 < \tau < 2$ can be reflected to the region $2 < \tau < \infty$ by Poisson summation.)
nodes.section: 8 Large value theorems for zeta partial sums

nodes.name: Asymptotic form of large value exponent at zeta
nodes.statement: Let $1/2 \leq \sigma \leq 1$, $\tau \geq 0$, and $\rho \geq 0$ be fixed. Then the following are equivalent: \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] $\LV_\zeta(\sigma,\tau) \leq \rho$. \item[(ii)] For every $\eps>0$ there exists $C,\delta>0$ such that if $(N,T,V,(a_n)_{n \in [N,2N]},J,W)$ is a zeta large value pattern with $N > C$, $N^{\tau-\delta} \leq T \leq N^{\tau+\delta}$, and $N^{\sigma-\delta} \leq V \leq N^{\sigma+\delta}$, then one has $$ |W| \leq C N^{\rho+\eps}.$$ \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 8 Large value theorems for zeta partial sums
equivalent_conditions: For every $\eps>0$ there exists $C,\delta>0$ such that
nodes.label: lvz-asymp

nodes.name: Proof of asymptotic form of LV_zeta
nodes.statement: The proof of Lemma \ref{lvz-asymp} proceeds as in previous sections and is omitted.
nodes.section: 8 Large value theorems for zeta partial sums

nodes.name: Basic properties of LV_zeta
nodes.statement: \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] (Monotonicity in $\sigma$) For any $\tau \geq 0$, $\sigma \mapsto \LV_\zeta(\sigma,\tau)$ is upper semicontinuous and monotone non-increasing. \item[(ii)] (Trivial bound) For any $1/2 \leq \sigma \leq 1$ and $\tau \geq 0$, we have $\LV_\zeta(\sigma,\tau) \leq \tau$. \item[(iii)] (Domination by large values) We have $\LV_\zeta(\sigma,\tau) \leq \LV(\sigma,\tau)$ for all $1/2 \leq \sigma \leq 1$ and $\tau \geq 0$. \item[(iv)] (Reflection) For $1/2 \leq \sigma \leq 1$ and $\tau > 1$, one has $$ \sup_{\sigma \leq \sigma' \leq 1} \LV_\zeta\left(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\tau-1} (\sigma'-\frac{1}{2}), \frac{\tau}{\tau-1}\right) + \frac{1}{\tau-1} (\sigma'-\sigma) = \frac{1}{\tau-1} \sup_{\sigma \leq \sigma' \leq 1} (\LV_\zeta(\sigma',\tau) + \sigma'-\sigma).$$ \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 8 Large value theorems for zeta partial sums
nodes.statement_short: $\LV_\zeta$ is monotone in $\sigma$, at most $\tau$, at most $\LV$, and satisfies a reflection identity $\tau\mapsto\tau/(\tau-1)$.
nodes.label: lvz-basic

nodes.name: Simplified reflection for LV_zeta
nodes.statement: We note that in practice, bounds for $\LV_\zeta(\sigma',\tau)+\sigma'$ are monotone decreasing\footnote{This reflects the fact that large value theorems usually relate to $p^{\mathrm{th}}$ moment bounds for $p \geq 1$ (e.g., $p = 2, 4, 6, 12$) rather than for $0 < p < 1$.} in $\sigma'$, so the reflection property in Lemma \ref{lvz-basic}(iv) morally simplifies\footnote{Alternatively, one can redefine $\LV_\zeta$ to use smooth cutoffs in the $n$ variable rather than rough cutoffs $1_I(n)$, in which case one can obtain the analogue of \eqref{lvz-reflect} rigorously, but we will not do so here.} to \begin{equation} \LV_\zeta\left(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\tau-1} (\sigma-\frac{1}{2}), \frac{\tau}{\tau-1}\right) = \frac{1}{\tau-1} \LV_\zeta(\sigma,\tau). \end{equation}
nodes.section: 8 Large value theorems for zeta partial sums
nodes.statement_short: Since bounds on $\LV_\zeta+\sigma'$ are usually decreasing in $\sigma'$, the reflection property morally reduces to (lvz-reflect).

nodes.name: Equation (8.1)
nodes.statement: \LV_\zeta\left(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\tau-1} (\sigma-\frac{1}{2}), \frac{\tau}{\tau-1}\right) = \frac{1}{\tau-1} \LV_\zeta(\sigma,\tau).
nodes.section: 8 Large value theorems for zeta partial sums
nodes.label: lvz-reflect

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: The claims (i), (ii) are obvious. The claim (iii) is clear by setting $a_n = 1_I$ in Definition \ref{lv-def}. Now we turn to (iv). By symmetry it suffices to prove the upper bound. Actually it suffices to just show $$ \LV_\zeta\left(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\tau-1} (\sigma-\frac{1}{2}), \frac{\tau}{\tau-1}\right) \leq \frac{1}{\tau-1} \sup_{\sigma \leq \sigma' \leq 1} (\LV_\zeta(\sigma',\tau) + \sigma'-\sigma)$$ as this easily implies the general upper bound. Let $(N,T,V,(a_n)_{n \in [N,2N]},J,W)$ be a zeta large value pattern with $N$ unbounded, $T= N^{\frac{\tau}{\tau-1}+o(1)}$, and $V = N^{\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\tau-1} (\sigma-\frac{1}{2})+o(1)}$. By definition, it suffices to show the bound \begin{equation} |W| \ll N^{\frac{1}{\tau-1} (\LV_\zeta(\sigma',\tau) + \sigma'-\sigma)+o(1)}. \end{equation} for some $\sigma \leq \sigma' \leq 1$. By definition, $a_n = 1_I(n)$.
